newsitem.title: USA: Success means trouble for many mutual funds.
newsitem.headline: Success means trouble for many mutual funds.

text.p: Since the beginning of 1996, investors have poured $269 billion into stock funds. The lion's share of that money has gone to the most successful funds of the past decade -- names such as Fidelity Magellan and Twentieth Century Ultra.
Trouble is, the funds' managers literally don't know what to do with all that money. As a result, many of the best-known mutual funds out there have been struggling lately.
Here's the problem: When a fund is small, it's easier to run. A manager can load up on his favourite stocks without worrying that his purchases will drive up the price of the shares.

By contrast, managers of giant funds with billions of dollars in assets can invest only a tiny percentage of their assets in any one stock, no matter how attractive it is. Often, such managers are forced to ignore small company shares altogether.
The result is that their portfolios occasionally are watered down with big, clunky stocks that the managers buy because they need to find something to do with their cash.

It's sad, really. The fund managers who are the best stock pickers sometimes end up running portfolios that look a lot like index funds. That's no fun for them -- and it's no fun for their shareholders, either.
Worse, some funds try to maintain their past records by making big bets on various sectors of the market.

Magellan is a prime example: As it grew larger, the fund found itself making large bets on individual market sectors such as technology, or even shifting to bonds in an attempt to time the market. That kind of thing is a long way from the fund's roots.
Former manager Peter Lynch made Magellan's reputation by picking individual stocks and he's written books that warn readers of the dangers of market timing.
Trouble is, many small funds stay small because they aren't very successful. So investors in search of excellence can't simply switch to funds with small asset bases.

Instead, they must look for funds that have stayed small despite their managers' ability to deliver sterling results -- bearing in mind that many good small funds are closed to new investors (that's how they stayed small).
A recent issue of Morningstar Investor, a monthly newsletter that covers the mutual fund industry, studied the problem and came up with a couple of strategies that might help you solve it.
The first strategy: Consider new funds whose portfolio managers have been successful elsewhere.

One example is Berger New Generation (800-333-1001; $2,000 minimum investment; 0.25 percent load), run by William R. Keithler. He previously managed Invesco Small Company Growth Fund, and delivered an annualized return from 1992 to 1993 of 24.6 percent vs. the average 14.9 percent return in the small-cap growth category.

Another idea is to find funds that don't do much marketing, or have high minimums that scare off investors. Morningstar points out five such funds. They include Torray (800-443-3036; $10,000 minimum; no load), which has delivered a 27.3 percent three-year annualized return. That performance puts it at the top of the 593 funds in its investment objective.
Fasciano (800-848-6050; $1,000 minimum; no load), has shown a 60 percent greater three-year return than its competitors, with 32 percent less risk.

The other three on their list are Mairs & Power Growth (800-304-7404; $2,500 minimum; no load); Papp America-Abroad (800-421-4004; $5,000 minimum; no load); and Sound Shore (800-551-1980; $10,000 minimum; no load).

Finally, one fund offers a new approach to the problem of size. Master's Select Equity (800-960-0188; $5,000 minimum; no load), managed by Ken Gregory, promises to close at a level that will preserve the focus of the fund.

But more important, it divides the fund's portfolio among six different top gun portfolio managers: Shelby Davis, Mason Hawkins, Spiros "Sig" Segalas, Foster Friess and team, Richard Weiss, and Jean-Marie Eveillard. Each manager will contribute his best 15 ideas. That way, shareholders won't be investing in any "filler" stocks that are little more than acceptable places to park a fund's cash.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
